title: What If Lightning Hit Your Plane? ⚡
description:
A bolt of lightning hits the plane Gus is asleep on, two miles up in a storm cloud, and the only thing he loses is his nap. This is where all that electricity goes, and what gets him in the end.

The numbers:
• A typical lightning flash carries about 30,000 amperes and heats the air to about 50,000 °F, five times the surface of the Sun (9,930 °F). An ordinary household circuit trips at 15 amperes: the bolt is 2,000 times that
• An airliner's skin is aluminium about 1 mm thick, thinner than a dime (1.35 mm). The current stays in that metal shell: in at one end, typically the nose or a wingtip, out at another, typically the tail
• Ohm's law for 30,000 A through a seamless aluminium tube the size of a 737 fuselage (38 m long, 3.76 m across, 1 mm skin): 0.19 milliohm, so about 6 volts from nose to tail. Real airframes have joints and are kept under about 2.5 milliohms, which would still be 75 volts: less than a 120-volt wall socket either way
• Airliners are struck about once a year each (one or two times, says the U.S. National Weather Service), mostly between 5,000 and 15,000 feet, and almost 90 % of the strikes are set off by the aircraft itself as it flies through a charged cloud
• A static spark has to be about 3,000 volts before you feel it. It carries less than a thousandth of a joule, which is why it only stings
(Assumptions: a typical flash, not the rare giant one; peak current; the skin alone, without frames and floor. Pilots still keep away from thunderstorms because of turbulence and hail, and every struck aircraft is inspected afterwards.)

Sources:
• U.S. National Weather Service, Lightning Safety: "How Powerful Is Lightning?", "How Hot Is Lightning?", "Lightning and Planes" (weather.gov/safety/lightning)
• E. J. Rupke, "What happens when lightning strikes an airplane?", Scientific American
• Flight Safety Foundation, AeroSafety World, June 2010 (aircraft-triggered strikes); SKYbrary, "Lightning" (5,000 to 15,000 ft)
• Fisher, Plumer and Perala, Aircraft Lightning Protection Handbook, DOT/FAA/CT-89/22; In Compliance Magazine, "Lightning and RF Electrical Bonding" (500 V at 200,000 A)
• Aluminium 2024-T3 resistivity (5.82e-8 ohm m); U.S. Mint coin specifications (dime 1.35 mm)

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
